To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Obama constituencies can be divided into two major groups, the first one consisting of the counties with high levels of education, high income and high percentage of college graduates, and the second one consisting of the rural counties with high percentage of African Americans, high percentage of people living below the poverty level, and low percentage of people with college education.

Obama was more likely to be supported in counties where the median household income was high and the population was young and educated; Obama was more likely supported in counties where median income was high and population was young but not necessarily educated; Obama was supported in the South where the median income was low and the population was older and more educated; and Obama was more likely be supported in the West where the median household was high and the populations was younger, less educated, and more Hispanic.
Obama's constituencies are characterized by (i) high levels of education, (ii) high levels of employment, (iii) high levels of homeownership, and (iv) high levels of income.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel method for mining discriminative patterns and with the demonstration of its application to a political data set, with a particular focus on the discovery of socio-economic patterns that are associated with support of Barack Obama in the presidential election of 2008.
the discovery of patterns that are associated with an outcome of interest, and that provide a concise summary of the underlying explanatory factors
the development of a data-centric framework that allows for the discovery of spatio-social motifs in election data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

Obama's support was based on a coalition of the young, the urban, and the educated, and on a more diverse set of constituencies, including the elderly, the rural, and the less-educated, but with a more limited geographical distribution.

the Obama support was concentrated in the counties that had high levels of education and high median incomes, but also in the counties that were relatively more urban, had a higher proportion of minorities and a lower proportion of people with a high school education.

Obama won the 2008 Presidential election by winning the support of a large, geographically widespread, and socio-economically diverse group of people, and a smaller, geographically more concentrated, and socio-econonically more homogeneous group.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proposed method can be used for discovering spatio-social motifs that explain the support of a political candidate in a given election.
our method provides a novel way to synthesize the information from the patterns into a small number that can be interpreted in terms of political geography.

the Obama support in 2008 was characterized by two main motifs: a large urban constituency and a small but widespread rural constituency, with the latter further divided into two smaller sub-constituents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proposed framework can be used to discover socio-economic patterns that are linked to electoral support in a data-driven manner, without any prior knowledge or assumptions.

association analysis provides a natural framework for discovering patterns of explanatory variables linked to a certain political outcome, and that the patterns can be synthesized into larger motifs that are interpretable in political terms.
association analysis provides a natural and effective framework for the discovery and characterization of spatio-social motifs in electoral data.
